experiences/oral-roberts-healing-crusade: Oral Roberts' tent healing crusades
Tulsa, Oklahoma

Paraphrase of Roberts' autobiographical accounts: healed of tuberculosis and stuttering as a teenager (1935), the Pentecostal Holiness preacher Oral Roberts launched healing campaigns in 1947 from Tulsa. In a huge tent seating thousands, he laid hands on long 'healing lines' of the sick, often praying against demons and disease. From 1955 his crusades were filmed for television, bringing Pentecostal healing into American living rooms.

Admirers saw a restoration of apostolic healing; journalists and doctors questioned unverified cures. Roberts later founded Oral Roberts University (1963), joined the United Methodist Church (1968) and taught 'seed faith' giving, an early form of prosperity theology. His 1987 appeal that God would 'call him home' unless he raised $8 million drew widespread criticism.
Pentecostal / charismatic
A key bridge from classical Pentecostalism to the Charismatic Renewal and televangelism; many credit his ministry with physical and spiritual healing.
Mainline Protestant
His move into Methodism symbolised growing mainline openness to charismatic practice, though many mainline clergy were critical of his methods.
Cessationist Reformed / evangelical critics
Critics such as John MacArthur challenge prosperity teaching and unverifiable healing claims.
Historian
David Harrell's biography shows a complex figure who moved from the tent revival to institution-building; historians link his 'seed faith' to the rise of the prosperity gospel.

Granville Oral Roberts was born in 1918 near Ada, Oklahoma, the son of a poor Pentecostal Holiness preacher; his mother had Choctaw ancestry. As a boy he stammered badly. At seventeen, in 1935, he collapsed with tuberculosis, which had killed relatives. According to his own often-repeated testimony, his brother took him to a tent revival in Ada, where the evangelist prayed for him; he said that he was healed of both the tuberculosis and the stammer that night, and that he heard God tell him he would take the message of healing to his generation.

For the next twelve years Roberts was a Pentecostal Holiness pastor and evangelist in Oklahoma, Georgia and North Carolina, and studied briefly at college. In 1947, while pastoring in Enid, Oklahoma, he reported being struck by the verse 3 John 2, with its wish that the reader 'prosper and be in health', and became convinced that God wanted people well and prosperous. He resigned his pastorate, held a healing meeting in Enid in May 1947, and moved to Tulsa, which became his base for the rest of his life. He began a magazine, Healing Waters (later Abundant Life), and a radio programme.

The campaigns grew quickly. Roberts bought a large tent, and by the 1950s his 'tent cathedral' could seat well over ten thousand people. The style was direct and physical. After a long sermon on faith, Roberts would sit at the front while a 'healing line' of the sick passed before him, sometimes for hours; he laid his right hand on each person and prayed, often commanding diseases and demons to leave. He encouraged a 'point of contact', an act of faith such as touching the radio or the magazine. In 1950 a windstorm in Amarillo, Texas, collapsed the tent during a service, but no one was killed, which supporters took as a sign of protection.

Roberts was one of the leading figures of the post-war 'healing revival' of the late 1940s and 1950s, alongside William Branham, Jack Coe, A.A. Allen and others associated with Gordon Lindsay's Voice of Healing network. In 1955 he began filming his crusades for television, showing the healing lines in American homes for the first time. Many viewers wrote in with testimonies; others were shocked. Journalists, doctors and some church leaders challenged the healing claims as unverified and accused him of exploiting the desperate. A 1956 crusade in Melbourne, Australia, was disrupted by hostile crowds and press criticism and ended early.

Roberts was less sensational than some of his colleagues and avoided the scandals that destroyed others. As the tent era waned in the 1960s he moved toward respectability: he founded Oral Roberts University in Tulsa, chartered in 1963, and in 1968 joined the United Methodist Church, to the dismay of many Pentecostals. He developed the teaching of 'seed faith', that gifts to God's work are seeds that God will multiply back to the giver, which became a foundation of later prosperity theology.

His later ventures drew more controversy. He built the City of Faith medical centre in Tulsa, opened in 1981 to combine prayer and medicine, which struggled financially and closed in 1989. In 1987 he told supporters that God would 'call him home' if he did not raise eight million dollars for medical scholarships; the money was raised, but the appeal was widely mocked and criticised. Roberts died in 2009, aged 91; his son Richard succeeded him and later resigned as university president in 2007 amid a financial scandal.

Oral Roberts brought Pentecostal healing out of rural tents and into mainstream American life through television, a university and his move into Methodism, helping make Pentecostal and charismatic Christianity respectable and paving the way for the charismatic renewal in older churches. His 'seed faith' teaching is widely regarded as a seedbed of the prosperity gospel, now influential across Africa, Latin America and Asia as well as the United States. Critics, including many evangelicals and Pentecostals, fault the lack of verification of healings, the financial appeals and the theology linking giving to material reward. Admirers stress his role in democratising prayer for the sick and in building lasting institutions.
experiences/william-branham-healing-revi: William Branham and the post-war healing revival
Jeffersonville, Indiana

Paraphrase of Branham's own accounts and campaign literature: Branham said that on 7 May 1946 an angel appeared to him and commissioned him to take a gift of healing to the world, with a sign of vibrations in his left hand that revealed diseases, and later the ability to discern people's names and secrets. His 1946-55 campaigns drew vast crowds in North America, Europe, South Africa and India. A 1950 photograph in Houston was promoted as showing a supernatural light above his head.

Branham is often regarded as the catalyst of the 1946-58 'Voice of Healing' revival, which included Oral Roberts, Jack Coe and A.A. Allen. In later years he taught the 'serpent seed' doctrine, baptism in Jesus' name only (Oneness theology) and his own role as an end-time Elijah; these teachings separated him from most Pentecostal churches. His followers ('Message' believers) remain numerous, especially in Africa.
Pentecostal / charismatic
Many credit his early ministry with genuine healings and prophetic accuracy, while rejecting his later doctrines; he is a cautionary example of gifting without sound teaching.
Trinitarian evangelical critics
His Oneness, serpent-seed and self-prophetic teachings are seen as heretical or cultic; his story is used to argue that miracles do not validate doctrine.
Historian
C. Douglas Weaver's study analyses Branham's charisma and the healing revival's mass-media methods; historians also note documented failed prophecies and contested healing claims.
Branhamite ('Message') believers
Regard him as the prophet of the last church age whose recorded sermons carry special authority.
Miracles vs. doctrine as a test of a prophet (cf. Deuteronomy 13).
Oneness theology and Nicene orthodoxy.
Charismatic personality cults.

William Marrion Branham was born in 1909 in a log cabin near Burkesville, Kentucky, into a very poor family that soon moved to Jeffersonville, Indiana, across the Ohio River from Louisville. In his later sermons he told of supernatural experiences from childhood: a light that appeared at his birth, and a voice from a whirlwind in a tree telling him not to drink, smoke or defile his body. Researchers have since noted that several of these autobiographical stories changed over time and are hard to corroborate. As a young man he was converted, ordained in an independent Baptist setting, and in 1933 began a small independent church in Jeffersonville, the Branham Tabernacle. In 1937 his wife and baby daughter died, a tragedy he described as a punishment for having refused, on others' advice, to associate with Pentecostals.

According to Branham, on 7 May 1946, while he was praying alone, an angel appeared and told him he had been sent to take a gift of divine healing to the peoples of the world. The angel promised two signs: a vibration in his left hand when he held a sick person's hand, revealing the disease, and later the ability to know the 'secrets of the heart'. Within weeks he held meetings in St Louis and among Oneness Pentecostals in the American South and West, where crowds reported dramatic healings.

From 1947 Gordon Lindsay became his campaign manager and in 1948 founded The Voice of Healing magazine to publicise the meetings. Branham's style was quiet and unpolished, in contrast to many evangelists. He would call people forward and, according to admirers, tell them details of their lives and illnesses before praying. His campaigns from 1946 to the mid-1950s drew huge crowds across North America and, from 1950, in Scandinavia, Britain, South Africa (1951), India (1954) and elsewhere. Reported healings included that of the former congressman William Upshaw, who said in 1951 that he could walk after decades of disability.

In January 1950, during a debate in Houston between Branham's associate F.F. Bosworth and a Baptist critic, a photographer hired by the critic's side took a picture showing a band of light above Branham's head. A document examiner, George Lacy, reported that the negative had not been retouched; Branham's followers have presented the photograph ever since as a picture of a supernatural light, while sceptics attribute it to lighting or a processing artefact.

Critics raised doubts at the time and later. Observers noted that people declared healed sometimes died soon afterwards, and that claims of raising the dead and of cures were rarely documented. The historian C. Douglas Weaver, among others, has examined the gap between Branham's accounts and the evidence. Branham's campaigns declined from the mid-1950s, and he faced a long dispute with the US tax authorities over his finances.

In his later years, preaching mostly at Jeffersonville, Branham developed teachings that separated him from most Pentecostals: the 'serpent seed' doctrine (that Eve's sin involved sexual union with the serpent, producing Cain's line), baptism in Jesus' name only, rejection of the doctrine of the Trinity as usually stated, condemnation of denominations as the mark of the beast, and strict rules on women's dress and roles. Many of his followers came to see him as the end-time prophet in the spirit of Elijah promised in Malachi 4. He predicted major end-time events around 1977. On 18 December 1965 his car was struck by a drunk driver in Texas, and he died on 24 December.

Branham is widely seen as the catalyst of the post-war American healing revival, and his style of 'word of knowledge' and discernment influenced later charismatic and Latter Rain movements and many healing evangelists. His later teachings, rejected by mainstream Pentecostals and outside Nicene Trinitarian orthodoxy, gave rise to the 'Message' movement, whose followers remain numerous, especially in Africa and Latin America. For critics he is a cautionary example of how reported miracles can lend authority to aberrant doctrine, often discussed with reference to Deuteronomy 13 and Matthew 7:22-23. Historians use his career to examine personality cults, the lack of accountability in independent healing ministries and the reliability of self-told life stories.
